title: Modi Puts Bihar's Plastic-to-Bench Recycling Model on National Stage
excerpt: During his 136th Mann Ki Baat address, PM Modi highlighted how Sitamarhi district turns 40 kg of single-use plastic waste into durable benches for schools and parks.
body:
• PM Modi praised Sitamarhi district's plastic recycling initiative during the 136th Mann Ki Baat on July 26, calling it a "waste to wealth" model
  • Each bench uses 40 kg of single-use plastic; 85 benches produced in the first phase from 4,000 kg of recycled waste
  • The district runs four processing units under Lohia Swachh Abhiyan in partnership with Buxar-based Rai Industries
  • Officials say the recycled benches cost Rs 2,000 less than conventional alternatives, making the model commercially sustainable

A Small District, a Big Shout-Out

Prime Minister Narendra Modi used his monthly radio address to spotlight a waste management experiment running in Bihar's Sitamarhi district, where single-use plastic — carry bags, wrappers, multilayer packaging — is being recycled into benches for government schools, parks and panchayat buildings.

Speaking during the 136th episode of Mann Ki Baat on Sunday, Modi described the initiative as a "magnificent example of waste to wealth" and said it showed that the principles of "Reduce, Reuse and Recycle" had moved beyond sloganeering into everyday practice.

"This is the PWMU Bajpatti unit, which is a designated processing centre. It is connected to three or four other blocks, and our network covers the entire Sitamarhi district."

— Raghav Jha, District Manager, Sitamarhi

How the Model Works

The district operates four Plastic Waste Management Units at Bajpatti, Runnisaidpur, Dumra and Riga under the state's Lohia Swachh Abhiyan programme. The facility at Bajpatti serves as the primary processing centre, receiving plastic collected from surrounding blocks.

The waste — mostly the low-value category that commercial recyclers typically reject — is cleaned, sorted, shredded into flakes, heated and moulded into dense structural sections that are assembled into benches. Each bench absorbs roughly 40 kilograms of plastic, according to district officials cited by YourStory.

The initiative is run as a commercial partnership between the Sitamarhi district administration and Rai Industries, a Buxar-based company, under a revenue-sharing arrangement. That structure is significant: most municipal plastic recovery schemes in India depend on subsidies, and models that fund their own collection economics tend to survive longer than those tied to individual officers or political cycles.

The Numbers So Far

In the first phase, about 8,000 kg of single-use plastic was collected from four blocks, of which 4,000 kg was recycled into 85 benches. Those benches have been distributed to government schools, rural panchayats and Panchayat Sarkar Bhawans across the district.

District officials told Patna Press that approximately 11,000 kg of plastic waste has been collected overall for processing at the Bajpatti unit, with daily collection running at 500 to 600 kg. Each recycled bench saves around Rs 2,000 compared to conventional alternatives, reducing procurement costs for the administration.

The Runnisaidpur facility is expected to begin manufacturing benches and other recycled furniture next month, according to Patna Press.

India's Plastic Problem in Context

India generates close to 39 lakh tonnes of plastic waste annually — roughly 10,700 tonnes a day — according to the Central Pollution Control Board's 2022-23 report. The country banned identified single-use plastic items from July 2022, but enforcement and collection remain uneven, particularly in smaller districts where formal waste infrastructure is thin.

The Extended Producer Responsibility framework already requires producers and brand owners to fund plastic packaging recovery, with obligations covering around 30 lakh tonnes in 2022-23. A district-level model that converts collected waste into a saleable product is precisely the kind of downstream capacity that EPR compliance money is designed to support.

Why It Matters Beyond Bihar

Modi's endorsement on a platform that reaches millions gives Sitamarhi's approach visibility that most district-level pilots never receive. For India's circular economy ecosystem — including startups, waste-tech ventures and diaspora investors interested in sustainable infrastructure — the signal is commercial as much as environmental.

A bench that pays for its own raw material through cost savings and revenue-sharing is a business proposition, not just a government pilot. District Magistrate Richie Pandey told reporters the initiative has the potential to generate employment by creating marketable products from recycled waste.

What's Next

The district administration plans to expand production of recycled furniture across all four processing units and is exploring additional product categories beyond benches. Whether the Sitamarhi model can be replicated in other districts — where waste collection logistics and industrial partnerships may differ — remains the central question. But with the Prime Minister's backing, the initiative now has the political tailwind that most municipal waste projects lack.
